items.title: Today's big AI models
items.subtitle: Today's big AI models have billions of knobs, some hundreds of billions.

items.title: Every step of training
items.subtitle: Every step of training, you need to know which way each knob should turn, and how far.

items.title: You'd never finish testing
items.subtitle: You'd never finish testing them one at a time.

items.title: The real trick?
items.subtitle: The real trick? One trip backward tells you how to turn every knob. It's called backpropagation.

items.title: Last time we saw that a neural
items.subtitle: Last time we saw that a neural network is layers of small units, each with its own knobs.

items.title: This time, we'll build a tiny network and watch
items.subtitle: This time, we'll build a tiny network and watch the error run backward through it, knob by knob.

items.title: In training, the model makes a guess
items.subtitle: In training, the model makes a guess, we compare it with the right answer, and the gap is the error.

items.title: The loss is a score for how wrong it is.
items.subtitle: The loss is a score for how wrong it is. Training is turning the knobs to push that score down.

items.title: Each knob's slope tells
items.subtitle: Each knob's slope tells you which way to turn, and how far. All the slopes together are the gradient.

items.title: The obvious way?
items.subtitle: The obvious way? Nudge one knob, rerun everything, and see if the error went up or down.

items.title: One full rerun per knob.
items.subtitle: One full rerun per knob. Billions of knobs, billions of reruns. For a single step.

items.title: Backpropagation starts at the answer instead.
items.subtitle: Backpropagation starts at the answer instead. Picture a chain of gears, with a pointer on the last one.

items.title: Turn the first gear one notch
items.subtitle: Turn the first gear one notch, and the second turns 2. Turn the second one notch, and the third turns 3.

items.title: So how far does the pointer move?
items.subtitle: So how far does the pointer move? Multiply along the way: 2 × 3. 6 notches.

items.title: So start at the pointer and work backward
items.subtitle: So start at the pointer and work backward, multiplying by each gear's ratio as you go.

items.title: At each gear you multiply once
items.subtitle: At each gear you multiply once and reuse what you already have. Nothing gets redone.

items.title: A neural network is a chain like this.
items.subtitle: A neural network is a chain like this. Each knob affects the answer through the layers after it. So the error can flow back the same way.

items.title: Here's a real, tiny network:
items.subtitle: Here's a real, tiny network: two layers, 7 knobs. It guesses taxi fares. We give it a 5-kilometer ride.

items.title: In the first layer, two units, A and B
items.subtitle: In the first layer, two units, A and B, use two knobs each to turn the five into a 6 and a 4.

items.title: The second layer
items.subtitle: The second layer multiplies each by a knob, adds a seventh knob, and guesses: 29 yuan.

items.title: The real fare was 23.
items.subtitle: The real fare was 23. 6 too high. That six is the error we pass back.

items.title: Last layer first.
items.subtitle: Last layer first. A knob's blame is the error times the number fed into it. That's its slope.

items.title: So: 6 × 6, 36.
items.subtitle: So: 6 × 6, 36. 6 × 4, 24. And the seventh knob's input is 1, so 6. Bigger input, bigger blame.

items.title: One layer back
items.subtitle: One layer back, the error flows along the wires and gets multiplied by each knob it passes.

items.title: For A, the error times 2: 12.
items.subtitle: For A, the error times 2: 12. For B, times 1: 6.

items.title: For their own two knobs
items.subtitle: For their own two knobs, it's error times input again.

items.title: One trip back
items.subtitle: One trip back, and all seven knobs have a number. We guessed high, so they all turn down, some more than others.

items.title: We turn each knob down
items.subtitle: We turn each knob down a little and guess again. 29 becomes about 24. Much closer.

items.title: We checked the slow way too:
items.subtitle: We checked the slow way too: one run with nothing changed, then one per nudged knob. 8 runs.

items.title: Same seven numbers, exactly.
items.subtitle: Same seven numbers, exactly. Backpropagation needed just one run forward and one trip back.

items.title: Scale up to a billion knobs
items.subtitle: Scale up to a billion knobs, and the slow way is 1,000,000,001 runs.

items.title: Even at one second a run
items.subtitle: Even at one second a run, that's over 30 years. For one step.

items.title: Backpropagation is still
items.subtitle: Backpropagation is still one trip each way. The trip back costs about two runs, so roughly 3 in all.

items.title: Without it, nobody could train these models.
items.subtitle: Without it, nobody could train these models.

items.title: So where does this come from?
items.subtitle: So where does this come from? In 1986, Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams laid it out in the journal Nature.

items.title: They found each knob's
items.subtitle: They found each knob's slope in two passes: forward, then back from the output.

items.title: They also found that the units
items.subtitle: They also found that the units in the middle learn to pick up useful patterns on their own.

items.title: Others had similar ideas earlier.
items.subtitle: Others had similar ideas earlier. This paper showed the method working on networks with several layers.

items.title: Today, in PyTorch
items.subtitle: Today, in PyTorch, a popular tool for building models, a single line does it: loss.backward(). Every knob gets its slope.

items.title: That's automatic differentiation.
items.subtitle: That's automatic differentiation. Underneath, it's backpropagation.

items.title: Backpropagation is passing
items.subtitle: Backpropagation is passing the blame backward, from the output, layer by layer.

items.title: One trip back
items.subtitle: One trip back, and every knob knows which way to turn, and how far.

items.title: But with so many knobs
items.subtitle: But with so many knobs, a model can memorize the practice questions and get new ones wrong.
